newsitem.title: UK: European bourses to break more records next year.
newsitem.headline: European bourses to break more records next year.

text.p: Europe's stock markets will continue to break records this year and next, strategists and economists said in a Reuters poll of forecasts published on Thursday.

Predictions for eight European bourses gathered this week showed Milan making the greatest gains by the end of this year, with Oslo and Frankfurt joining it with strong performances in 1997. "It's financial market heaven," said David Aserkoff, vice-president and equity strategist at CS First Boston in London.
"The economic outlook is about as good as it gets for equities," said Peter Sullivan, European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs in London.

New peaks for stock markets across Europe this week were fuelled by receding fears of monetary tightening in the U.S. which briefly sent the Dow Jones above the 6,000 level for the first time on Monday this week.
The poll saw share markets in Germany, Netherlands, Norway and Sweden beating records seen in the past week and closing 1996 at all-time highs.
Over 70 percent of forecasts predicted a stock market rise between now and the end of 1996 for all countries except for Switzerland and Britain.
Around 75 percent of respondents expected the Swiss and British bourses to close lower than current levels at the end of 1996.
In all markets in 1997, bulls outnumbered bears by almost four to one.
Reuters collected 149 forecasts. Some institutions gave forecasts for more than one country.
In France and Italy, the closing levels of the CAC-40 and BCI General indices at the end of 1996 would be highs for the year.

"The European bourses have done extraordinarily well, driven by falling interest rates, a slightly better economic growth outlook and ongoing gains in the U.S. stock market," said CS First Boston's Aserkoff.
In terms of percentage changes from current levels, the greatest strides are likely to be in Italy over the next two years, according to the poll.

The average of six forecasts for Milan's BCI General Index predicted a 21 percent gain to around 760 points by December 1997 after about 9.5 percent growth at the end of 1996 from Wednesday's close of 629.19.
Traders attributed this to confidence in the Olive Tree coalition's tight budget which they said would encourage investors to switch from government stocks to equities.
"The government will bring more confidence and ... cause the market to tick up," said Oriano Moro, trader at Gestnord in Milan.
Strategists predicted Germany's DAX-30 index would grow by 2.2 percent by the end of the year, and by 11.5 percent by the end of 1997.
"We're looking at strong economic growth in Europe as a whole and Germany is the most cyclical market in Europe, so the business cycle is very positive," said Sullivan at Goldman Sachs.

The Oslo Total Index, which closed at 871.57 on Wednesday, is expected to grow by 2.9 percent between now and the end of the year, and by 16.4 percent to around 1,015 by the end of next year, the poll showed.
"I dont believe the European economy will peak until 1998," said one analyst in Oslo. "I see no grounds for a crash."
France's CAC-40 was expected to rise to around 2,180 by the end of 1996 and 2,230 by end 1997.
"We're very bullish about the French market," said Jaques Chahine, chairman of Jaques Chahine Finance in Paris, who based his forecasts on lower interest rates and a more robust economy in 1997.
Sweden's General index would beat its record high of 2,140.61 set on Tuesday, climbing to around 2,230 by the end of this year, the poll showed.
Other indices were expected to consolidate before resuming their upward path, strategists said.

London's FTSE-100 -- the largest European bourse -- would dip by 2.3 percent to around 3,900 before the end of the year as political uncertainty ahead of the UK's forthcoming election took its toll, strategists said.
The Swiss Market Index (SMI) was seen dipping to around 3,760 by the end of this year with worries over interest rate hikes putting a lid on much near-term growth.
